261.quote_or_event: “Fareed, do not turn around and strike those who strike you with their fists. Kiss their feet, and return to your own home.”
261.explanation: Shaikh Farid, whose saloks are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, tells the seeker to take blows without hitting back, to answer them with humility, and to return to inner peace.
261.tie_back: Valluvar defines true penance as bearing what one suffers while causing no suffering to others; Farid asks for exactly that, patience under blows and no retaliation.
261.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid 7 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
261._accuracy_note: Strong fit for both halves of the definition (endure, do not inflict), though Farid does not call this tapas and Sikhism itself rejects formal penance.

262.quote_or_event: “Yoga is not the patched coat, Yoga is not the walking stick. Yoga is not smearing the body with ashes.”
262.explanation: In Raag Soohee Guru Nanak tells the yogis that the ascetic's coat, staff and ash do not make a person one with God; union comes from living purely in the midst of the world.
262.tie_back: The Kural says putting on the outward form of penance is futile without the inner quality; Guru Nanak likewise empties the ascetic's outfit of any value.
262.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 730, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
262._accuracy_note: Strong fit on outward form being futile, but the Kural's other reading (penance as fruit of merit from past births) has no counterpart, and Guru Nanak rejects ascetic practice more broadly than Valluvar.

263.quote_or_event: “One who calls himself a guru or a spiritual teacher, while he goes around begging - don't ever touch his feet. One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
263.explanation: In Vaar Saarang Guru Nanak refuses honour to holy men who live by begging and gives it instead to the householder who earns by his own labour and shares what he has.
263.tie_back: Valluvar wonders, perhaps ironically, whether householders have stopped doing penance because they are busy feeding renunciants; Guru Nanak answers that honest work and sharing (kirat karni, vand chhakna) is itself the true path.
263.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Vaar Saarang (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
263._accuracy_note: Same theme of householder and renunciant, but Sikhism reverses the Kural's premise: it values the working householder over the begging ascetic, which only suits the ironic reading of this couplet.

264.quote_or_event: “He Himself is the Supreme Master of all; wealth and miraculous spiritual powers, and all other external tastes and pleasures, are all like beads on a string.”
264.explanation: In Japji Guru Nanak tells the yogis that God alone is Master, and that the occult powers (siddhis) they seek through austerity are only side pleasures.
264.tie_back: The Kural credits the ascetic with power to destroy enemies and raise friends; Guru Nanak places all such power in God and treats yogic powers as distractions.
264.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji Sahib, Pauri 29, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
264._accuracy_note: Next-best and partly opposed: Sikhism rejects the idea that austerity gives a person power to curse or bless, so the verse addresses the Kural's theme mainly by contrast.

265.quote_or_event: “In the remembrance of God, hopes are fulfilled.”
265.explanation: In the Sukhmani Guru Arjan lists the fruits of simran, meditative remembrance of God, and among them says that a person's hopes are fulfilled.
265.tie_back: Valluvar urges penance now because it gives whatever one desires; Guru Arjan makes the same promise for remembering God.
265.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 263, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
265._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the promise matches, but the means is naam simran rather than tapas, the urgency of 'here and now' is absent, and Sikh commentators (e.g. Sahib Singh) often read 'fulfilled' as the mind being freed of craving.

266.quote_or_event: “This human body has been given to you. This is your chance to meet the Lord of the Universe. Nothing else will work.”
266.explanation: Guru Arjan tells the listener that human birth is the one opportunity to meet God, and that every other pursuit is useless for that purpose.
266.tie_back: The Kural says those who practise penance alone do their real work while everyone else labours for their own ruin; Guru Arjan likewise calls seeking God the one work that counts and the rest useless.
266.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa (So Purakh section; also at Ang 378), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
266._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the one true task versus wasted effort, though Guru Arjan's path is meditation within the sangat, not tapas, and the 'net of desire' image is not used.

267.quote_or_event: “Let self-control be the furnace, and patience the goldsmith. … With the Fear of God as the bellows, fan the flames of tapa, the body's inner heat.”
267.explanation: The closing pauri of Japji describes the spiritual life as a goldsmith's workshop, where self-control is the furnace and tapa the fire in which the true Word is forged.
267.tie_back: Valluvar compares the ascetic to gold that shines brighter the more it burns; Guru Nanak also uses the goldsmith's fire and names tapa as the heat that does the work.
267.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8, Japji Sahib, Pauri 38, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
267._accuracy_note: Strong imagery match (goldsmith, fire, tapa), but in Japji the fire forges the Word in a mint rather than purifying a person through suffering; the ellipsis marks one omitted line.

268.quote_or_event: “Among all persons, the supreme person is the one who gives up his egotistical pride in the Company of the Holy.”
268.explanation: In the Sukhmani Guru Arjan says the greatest of all people is the one whose ego (haumai) has been erased in holy company.
268.tie_back: The Kural says the one who has lost the sense of 'I' and 'mine' is worshipped by all; Guru Arjan likewise ranks the ego-free person above everyone.
268.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 266, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
268._accuracy_note: Strong fit: losing ego leads to supreme standing in both; Gurbani credits the sangat rather than austerity, and speaks of pre-eminence rather than worship by all creatures.

269.explanation: In the opening section of the Sukhmani Guru Arjan says that remembering God drives death away.
269.tie_back: The Kural says those with the power of penance can leap even beyond Death; Guru Arjan says the same for one who remembers God.
269.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 262, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 1, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
269._accuracy_note: Strong fit on overcoming death, but the means is simran, not tapas-power, and Sikh commentators (e.g. Sahib Singh) read it as the fear of death being removed.

270.quote_or_event: “Out of millions, hardly anyone is a servant of the Lord. All the others are mere traders.”
270.explanation: In Raag Gujri Guru Arjan observes that among millions there is scarcely one true devotee, while the rest practise religion as a bargain for their own gain.
270.tie_back: Valluvar explains the world's want by noting that those who practise are few and those who do not are many; Guru Arjan makes the same observation about true devotees and the many who only trade.
270.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 495, Raag Gujri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
270._accuracy_note: Reasonable: the few-versus-many contrast matches closely, but Guru Arjan does not draw the Kural's causal link to the world's poverty or weakness.
